Linear and polynomial regression, for programmers

Least squares for real: normal equations, projections, numerical stability, inference, bias-variance and regularization. With verified code and an example worked by hand.

Summary

  • Polynomial regression is linear regression: the model is linear in the parameters , even though it is polynomial in . You only need to change the columns of .
  • The least-squares solution is the orthogonal projection of onto the column space of .
  • In code, never invert : use QR or SVD (lstsq) and scale . Vandermonde matrices are terribly conditioned.
  • With Gaussian noise, least squares is maximum likelihood, and you get confidence and prediction intervals in closed form.
  • The degree is chosen with cross-validation, not with . Ridge controls the variance of high degrees.
features φ(x)→ matrix X→ QR / SVD→ β̂, σ̂²→ intervals↺ CV picks degree and λ

§1 · The model

Linear in the parameters, not in x

Simple linear regression models each observation as a straight line plus noise:

Polynomial regression of degree just adds powers of :

The key point: are known numbers once you have the data. The unknowns appear linearly. Stacking the equations in matrix form with the (Vandermonde) design matrix:

This generalizes to any fixed transformation (logarithms, sines, splines, multi-column features): . Everything that follows still holds. "Linear" refers to .

§2 · Least squares

The loss function and the normal equations

We choose by minimizing the residual sum of squares (RSS):

is a convex quadratic in , with Hessian . Setting the gradient to zero:

These are the normal equations. If has full column rank ( and linearly independent columns), is invertible and the solution is unique:

In the simple case () it reduces to the high-school formulas:

Below is the surface for the taxi data from the simple version. Click anywhere on the map to set and see the corresponding line, or launch gradient descent from there.

The valley is long, narrow and diagonal: and are correlated because . Gradient descent zigzags down it. Centering (subtracting ) makes the valley round and convergence immediate. It's the same reason features get scaled before training almost any model.

§3 · Geometry

Least squares is an orthogonal projection

Every possible prediction is a linear combination of the columns of , so it lives in the subspace (dimension ). The data vector is in general not in that subspace. The point of closest to is its orthogonal projection:

The normal equations say exactly that the residual is perpendicular to every column:

Two practical consequences. First: the diagonal element of is the leverage of point : how hard it pulls on its own prediction. Points with extreme have high leverage, and in high-degree polynomials the edges have enormous leverage. Second: , the degrees of freedom the model uses up.

§4 · Implementation

Solving it properly: QR, SVD and scaling

Forming squares the condition number: . With you already lose all 16 digits of a float64. The standard alternative is the QR factorization, with and upper triangular:

One back substitution and you're done, with error proportional to instead of . np.linalg.lstsq uses SVD, which also handles rank-deficient matrices (it returns the minimum-norm solution via the pseudoinverse ).

But the Vandermonde matrix is ill-conditioned from the start. Condition number of with 50 speeds between 0 and 120 km/h:

Degree draw x [0, 120]x scaled to [−1, 1]Chebyshev basis on [−1, 1]
11.4 × 10²1.71.7
21.9 × 10⁴3.61.8
32.5 × 10⁶7.92.2
54.0 × 10¹⁰412.4
86.6 × 10¹⁶ (useless)5202.5
122.4 × 10²⁷1.6 × 10⁴2.5

Rule of thumb: always scale to (or standardize it) before building powers. For high degrees use an orthogonal basis (Chebyshev, Legendre) with numpy.polynomial. The predictions are identical; only the parametrization changes.

ols.py · NumPy, verified against np.linalg.lstsq and statsmodels (differences < 1e-14)

import numpy as np

def design(x, d, lo, hi):
    u = (2 * x - (lo + hi)) / (hi - lo)           # scale to [-1, 1]
    return np.vander(u, d + 1, increasing=True)   # columns [1, u, u^2, ..., u^d]

def ols(X, y):
    Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)                        # X = QR, without forming X^T X
    beta = np.linalg.solve(R, Q.T @ y)            # R beta = Q^T y
    resid = y - X @ beta
    n, p = X.shape
    s2 = resid @ resid / (n - p)                  # unbiased estimator of sigma^2
    Rinv = np.linalg.inv(R)                       # p x p, small
    cov_beta = s2 * Rinv @ Rinv.T                 # = s2 (X^T X)^-1
    return beta, s2, cov_beta

X = design(x, 2, lo=0.0, hi=10.0)
beta, s2, cov_beta = ols(X, y)

§5 · Probability

The statistical view: maximum likelihood and intervals

Assume i.i.d. Gaussian noise, . The log-likelihood is

Maximizing it over is exactly minimizing : least squares = MLE with Gaussian noise. Without assuming normality, the Gauss-Markov theorem guarantees that is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) if the errors have zero mean, constant variance and are uncorrelated.

§6 · Metrics

R², adjusted R² and RMSE

Careful: training never goes down when you add columns, because the subspace only grows and the projection can only get closer to . With it is exactly 1. The adjusted version penalizes parameters, but to choose a model the right thing is to measure on data the model hasn't seen.

§7 · Choosing the degree

Bias, variance and cross-validation

If the data come from , the expected error at a new point breaks down into three terms:

The degree shifts the balance: low degree, high bias (it can't represent ); high degree, high variance (each dataset gives a different curve). The widget simulates 30 different datasets with the same (dashed) and the same noise level, and fits a polynomial to each one:

112

In practice is unknown, so the generalization error is estimated with k-fold cross-validation: you split the data into blocks, train on and measure on the remaining one, rotating.

For least squares, leave-one-out has a closed form and you don't need to retrain times: .

§8 · Regularization

Ridge: penalizing large coefficients

Overfitting polynomials have huge coefficients that cancel each other out. Ridge adds an penalty:

is always invertible for , so it also fixes the ill-conditioning. In SVD terms (), ridge shrinks each direction by a factor : poorly determined directions (small ) get switched off. In Bayesian terms it's the MAP with prior , and the posterior mean matches that of a GP with kernel . The intercept is not penalized, and the features must be scaled.

Lasso uses : it has no closed form, but it drives coefficients exactly to zero (feature selection). Degree 12 on 15 points:

10⁻⁸ (unregularized)10²

§9 · Beyond

Extensions you'll use in real life

  • Multiple regression. Several input variables are just more columns in . A polynomial of degree in variables with interactions has terms: it blows up fast.
  • Splines. Instead of one global high-degree polynomial, piecewise cubic polynomials joined smoothly at knots. They avoid Runge's phenomenon (oscillations at the edges) and are still least squares with a different basis.
  • Weighted least squares. If the noise variance changes with (heteroscedasticity), with .
  • Robust regression. The squared loss is very sensitive to outliers (a residual of 10 weighs 100). Huber or absolute loss (HuberRegressor, IRLS) dampens them.
  • Generalized linear models. Swapping the Gaussian likelihood for a Bernoulli one and the identity for the sigmoid gives you logistic regression, the next chapter of the series.

§10 · Assumptions

Diagnosing the residuals

The intervals from §5 are only valid if the assumptions hold. You check them by looking at the residuals, not the coefficients:

AssumptionWhat it looks like when it failsRemedy
Linearity (correct shape)Residuals vs. with a U or S patternRaise the degree, splines, transform
Constant varianceFunnel-shaped residualsTransform (log), WLS, robust errors (HC3)
IndependenceResiduals correlated in time (streaks)Time-series models, HAC errors
Normality (only for intervals with small n)Curved Q-Q plot, heavy tailsBootstrap, robust regression
No multicollinearityUnstable coefficients, VIF > 10Drop variables, ridge, PCA
No influential pointsHigh Cook's distance, Check the data point; robust regression

§11 · In production

With libraries

scikit-learn · choosing degree and λ with cross-validation

import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

for d in [1, 2, 3, 8]:
    model = make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),                         # scale x before the powers
        PolynomialFeatures(d),
        StandardScaler(),                         # scale the powers for ridge
        RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-6, 3, 30)),   # picks lambda by internal CV
    )
    rmse = -cross_val_score(model, x.reshape(-1, 1), y, cv=5,
                            scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean()
    print(d, round(rmse, 3))      # on the test data: 0.75, 0.346, 0.363, 0.371 -> degree 2

statsmodels · coefficient table, standard errors and intervals

import statsmodels.api as sm

res = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()          # X from design(): already includes the column of ones
print(res.summary())              # beta, standard errors, t, p-values, R^2, adjusted R^2
pred = res.get_prediction(design(np.array([5.0]), 2, 0.0, 10.0))
print(pred.summary_frame(alpha=0.05))
# mean_ci_lower / mean_ci_upper -> confidence interval
# obs_ci_lower  / obs_ci_upper  -> prediction interval

§12 · Checklist

Before you trust your regression

  • Plot the data and the residuals. A pattern in the residuals means a misspecified model.
  • Scale to before building powers; for degree ≥ 6 use an orthogonal basis or splines.
  • Solve with lstsq / QR. No inv(X.T @ X).
  • Choose degree and with cross-validation, never with the training .
  • Report prediction intervals if you're going to make decisions about individual observations.
  • Don't extrapolate: outside the range of , the leverage and uncertainty of a polynomial grow like .
  • Look for influential points (leverage, Cook's distance) before believing a slope.
  • Remember that a significant coefficient is association, not causation.

§13 · Worked example

At what speed does a truck use the least fuel?

We'll do everything by hand with 5 data points, to see every formula on this page working on a real fleet problem.

The setup. A company has 50 trucks that each cover 120,000 km a year, currently with an internal speed limit of 100 km/h. They measured the average consumption of a typical truck on flat stretches at constant speed. They want to know: what is the most efficient speed, and how much would they save by lowering the limit to 85 km/h?

Speed vConsumption yu (new scale, see step 2)
50 km/h34.5 L/100 km−2
65 km/h32.0 L/100 km−1
80 km/h32.9 L/100 km0
95 km/h34.0 L/100 km1
110 km/h38.2 L/100 km2

Example map

We want a U-shaped curve that passes as close as possible to the 5 points. A parabola has 3 knobs; least squares picks them by solving 3 simple equations.

  1. Look at the data and choose the shape.
  2. Rescale the speed so the arithmetic is easy.
  3. Build a table of sums (like in a spreadsheet).
  4. Solve the 3 equations by substitution.
  5. Check the errors and how much the curve explains.
  6. Find the most efficient speed.
  7. Work out how much to trust the prediction, and decide.

  1. Look at the data and choose the shape

    In words

    The truck uses more fuel at 50 than at 65 (low gears, engine outside its sweet spot) and much more at 110 (air resistance grows very quickly with speed). There's a minimum somewhere in between. A straight line can't go down and then up; a parabola can.

    The model

    Three knobs: is the consumption at 80 km/h, the slope (whether it goes up or down as you speed up) and how much the curve bends. The is the speed written on a handier scale; step 2 explains exactly what it is.

  2. Rescale the speed

    In words

    With the raw speed, the squared term reaches : huge numbers and error-prone arithmetic (§4 explains why the same thing happens to the computer). So instead of using the speed as is, we measure it with a different ruler: how many 15 km/h steps we are above or below 80 km/h. We call that number .

    The math

    v (km/h)50658095110
    u−2−1012

    Where do the 80 and the 15 come from?

    80 is the middle speed of the measurements (50, 65, 80, 95, 110): subtracting it makes the center of the data 0. 15 is the gap between one measurement and the next: dividing by 15, each measurement ends up one step from its neighbor. They aren't magic numbers: any center and any step size would give the same curve, just with uglier arithmetic. We pick the ones that leave whole numbers.

    What it means: same data, small numbers, symmetric around zero. That will make many sums equal zero. To go back you just undo the change: . That's why is the consumption at 80 km/h: at 80 km/h, and the other two terms vanish.

  3. The table of sums

    In words

    Least squares only needs a few sums of the data. It's exactly what you'd do in a spreadsheet: one column for each power of ( is , is …) and its product with the consumption , plus a row of totals (, "sum of the whole column"). Step 4 shows what each total is for.

The zeros come from having centered the speed in step 2: the negative values cancel the positive ones.

    answers: of all the variation (TSS), what fraction stops being error when you use the curve? 1 = perfect; 0 = no better than always using the average.

  6. The most efficient speed

    In words

    The bottom of the U is where the curve stops going down and starts going up, that is, where its slope is zero. For a parabola there's a direct formula: the slope of is , and that of is (the power rule for derivatives: bring the 2 down and subtract one from the exponent).

    The math

    And to get back to km/h we undo step 2 ():

    That is, 72.7 km/h and 32.15 L/100 km.

    What it means: according to this data, the truck uses the least fuel at about 73 km/h.

  7. How much can we trust it? Intervals for 85 km/h

    In words

    Three ingredients: the typical error of one measurement, how far we are from the center of the data, and a multiplier that penalizes having little data.

    The math

    1. Typical error of one measurement. We spread the sum of squared errors over the "degrees of freedom": 5 data points minus the 3 knobs we already used = 2.

    2. How much the noise shows at that point. At 85 km/h, . The "leverage" says what fraction of the measurement noise leaks into the curve at that point. In §5 it's ; with the sums from step 3, for this data that formula becomes something you can do on a calculator:

    (At the ends, at 50 or 110 km/h, : the curve is held much less firmly there.)

    3. Multiplier for having little data. For 95% you use the Student's t table with 2 degrees of freedom: 4.30 (in Excel T.INV.2T(0.05, 2), in Python t.ppf(0.975, 2)). With lots of data it would be close to 2; with so little you have to be much more cautious.

    The prediction itself, with :

    Average consumption at 85 km/h:

    One specific trip at 85 km/h (the noise of that trip is added, the “1+”):

    What it means: the average consumption at 85 km/h is, with 95% confidence, between 31.3 and 34.3. A specific trip can vary more (30.1 to 35.5). The intervals are wide because there are only 5 measurements: with more measured stretches they would narrow a lot.

  8. Turning it into a decision

    In words

    At 85 km/h the curve gives 32.80 L/100 km (step 7). At 100 km/h, with , it gives:

    The difference is per 100 km; we multiply it by the kilometers of the whole fleet:

    The math

    About 153,500 liters a year.

    Cost in time: the same million km, driven at 85 instead of 100 (hours = km ÷ speed):

    more hours of driving per year. Savings per extra hour: liters.

    What it means: lowering the limit to 85 pays off if one hour of driver and truck costs less than 14.5 liters of diesel. Going all the way down to the 73 km/h optimum makes no sense: near the bottom the curve is flat, and almost all the savings are already achieved at 85, without as many extra hours.

45 km/h115 km/h

consumo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

v = np.array([50, 65, 80, 95, 110.])              # km/h
y = np.array([34.5, 32.0, 32.9, 34.0, 38.2])      # L/100 km
u = (v - 80) / 15                                 # scaled: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2
X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(u), u, u**2])

res = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
b0, b1, b2 = res.params                           # 32.377, 0.940, 0.971
u_opt = -b1 / (2 * b2)
print(f"v* = {80 + 15*u_opt:.1f} km/h, R2 = {res.rsquared:.3f}")   # v* = 72.7 km/h, R2 = 0.976

u85 = (85 - 80) / 15
frame = res.get_prediction(np.array([[1, u85, u85**2]])).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
print(frame.round(2).to_string())
# mean 32.80 | mean_ci 31.27-34.33 | obs_ci 30.09-35.51

ahorro = (res.predict([[1, 4/3, 16/9]]) - res.predict([[1, u85, u85**2]]))[0] / 100 * 50 * 120_000
print(f"{ahorro:,.0f} L/year")                    # 153,543 L/year

What would change in a real system

  • Much more data: telemetry gives thousands of stretches per truck; with that the intervals narrow dramatically.
  • More variables: load, grade, wind and temperature. They're added as columns (multiple regression), with interactions such as speed × load.
  • Per-vehicle effects: each truck has its own curve; a mixed model or a per-vehicle term captures that.
  • Physical shape: aerodynamic drag goes with in force, and consumption per distance reflects it; a physics-based model (rolling + aerodynamics) can extrapolate better than a free polynomial.
  • Validation: choose degree and variables with cross-validation by truck or by route, not by row, so no information leaks between training and test.
